This interactive demo builds a patient's digital twin with
`simulateTrajectory()`, as in [Digital twins](digital-twins.html), and
runs in the browser with no R needed. Pick a patient from the `pbc3`
data, or upload one patient's follow-up visits as a CSV file. The
interface is available in English and Chinese.

<iframe src="https://wenhaoli18.shinyapps.io/bjm-twin/"
        style="width: 100%; height: 1550px; border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 6px;"
        title="BJM digital twin demo" loading="lazy"></iframe>

If the frame does not load, [open the demo in a new tab](https://wenhaoli18.shinyapps.io/bjm-twin/).
On the free hosting plan the app goes to sleep when nobody is using it, so
the first visit can take up to a minute to start.

## What the demo shows

The app fits the sub-models once, when it starts, on `pbc3`: a Cox model
for death or transplantation (`status3`), a logistic model for which of
the two occurred (`status4`), and linear mixed models for three biomarkers
(log serum bilirubin, albumin and log prothrombin time). The twin is a set
of futures drawn from the model, conditional on the patient's
measurements up to the year it is built at.

**Replay the twin.** Move the "Twin built at year" slider, or press its
play button, and the twin is rebuilt from the measurements up to that
year. The forecast biomarker is shown as a median and 90% band. The
measurements the twin used are filled points, and the ones taken later
are open points, so you can see how the forecast compares with what
happened. Next to it are the forecast probabilities of death and of
transplantation. For the example patients, the patient's actual outcome
is marked as well.

**Ask the twin.** A sample of the simulated futures is drawn as one line
each, ending at its event. The twin then answers questions from all of
its futures:

- the probability of death, of transplantation, or of either, within a
  chosen number of years;
- the probability that a biomarker goes above or below a threshold before
  any event, and the probability that the patient is event-free and past
  the threshold at a chosen time;
- the median year of the event, and the probability of being event-free
  through the end of the forecast.

**Trial design.** This tab looks at all of `pbc3` rather than one
patient, and follows [Twins in a randomized
trial](digital-twins.html#twins-in-a-randomized-trial): each participant's
twin is built from their baseline measurements alone, and its prediction
of the trial's endpoint is used as a covariate in the analysis (the idea
behind PROCOVA). Because the prediction uses only data from before
randomization, the adjustment leaves the treatment effect unbiased and
shrinks its variance by a factor of 1 - ρ², where ρ is the correlation
between the prediction and the outcome. Choose the endpoint (a biomarker
at year 1 to 5, or death or transplantation within that many years), the
treatment effect (a difference in means in standard deviations of the
outcome, or a relative risk reduction), the significance level and the
power. The app shows ρ as estimated on `pbc3`, the total sample size of a
1:1 trial with and without the twin as a covariate, and how many fewer
participants the adjusted trial needs. Adjusting for the baseline value
alone is shown for comparison, together with a plot of the twins'
predictions against the observed outcomes and of the sample size across
treatment effects. The twins are fit on the same `pbc3` data, outcomes
included, so ρ is optimistic: the tab illustrates the idea and is not a
tool for designing a real trial.

The twin is a statistical, predictive model of outcomes as observed in
the data it was fit on, not a mechanistic or causal model of the disease.

## Uploading a patient

The CSV needs one row per visit and the columns `year`, `age`, `sex`,
`serBilir`, `albumin` and `prothrombin`, on the same scales as `pbc3`.
The app has a template you can download. Visits after the year the twin
is built at are not used by the twin, but are shown as open points.

## Running the app locally

The app's source is in the
[`shiny/bjm-twin`](https://github.com/wenhaoli18/BJM/tree/master/shiny/bjm-twin)
folder of the repository. To run it on your own computer, clone the
repository and run:

```r
install.packages(c("shiny", "bslib"))
shiny::runApp("shiny/bjm-twin")
```

The demo is for illustrating the method only. Its models are fit on the
PBC data set and must not be used for clinical decisions.
